tips.title: The order, and the two non-metals in it
tips.body: **potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron, copper**, most reactive first. **Carbon** sits between magnesium and zinc, and **hydrogen** between iron and copper. Those two placements are what make the series useful rather than just a list.

tips.title: Reactivity is how readily it forms a positive ion
tips.body: When a metal reacts, its atoms **form positive ions**. The more readily a metal does that — the more easily it **loses electrons** — the **more reactive** it is. Every trend in this topic is that one sentence applied.

tips.title: Copper sits below hydrogen, so acid does nothing
tips.body: A metal only displaces hydrogen from an acid if it is **above hydrogen** in the series. **Copper is below**, so copper and dilute acid **do not react** — the standard question, and the answer is the position, not the metal being unreactive in general.

tips.title: Displacement works downwards only
tips.body: A **more** reactive metal displaces a **less** reactive one from its compound. Magnesium takes copper out of copper sulfate; copper cannot take magnesium out of magnesium sulfate. If your predicted reaction runs up the series, it does not happen.

tips.title: Oxidation is gain of oxygen here
tips.body: In this spec point, **oxidation is gain of oxygen** and **reduction is loss of oxygen**. The electron definition (OIL RIG) is the **Higher tier** version and comes next. Use whichever the question is written in.

why.matters:
Reactivity is one property, not a list: how readily a metal gives up its outer electrons to become a positive ion. Order the metals by it and three separate practical questions answer themselves at once.

Which metal will push another out of its compound. Which metals fizz in acid and which sit there. And — the one that shaped history — how a metal has to be got out of the ground, because the ones that hold their electrons loosely are exactly the ones that will not let go of their oxygen.

examples.title: Why gold is panned and aluminium is electrolysed
examples.body:
Gold is found as gold. It is so unreactive that it never combined with anything, so it sits in a river bed as metal and can be picked out with a pan.

Everything more reactive is found as a **compound**, and how much trouble it is to extract runs straight down the reactivity series. Metals below carbon can be reduced by heating with it, which is a furnace and some coke. Metals above carbon hold their oxygen too tightly for that, and need **electrolysis** — which is why aluminium waited for cheap electricity.

visual.alt: A table running down the reactivity series: aluminium found as an oxide and extracted by electrolysis, iron and copper found as ores and reduced by heating with carbon, and gold found as the metal itself

examples.title: Why water pipes are copper
examples.body:
A metal displaces hydrogen from an acid only if it is **above hydrogen** in the series. Zinc is above it, so zinc and dilute acid fizz. Copper is below it, so copper and dilute acid do nothing at all.

That single position is why copper carries drinking water, sits on roofs for a century and gets made into coins. It is not that copper is inert — it tarnishes in air and dissolves in the right acid — but against the weak acids in water it has no tendency to give up electrons.

visual.alt: Two rows: zinc, which sits above hydrogen in the reactivity series, reacting with hydrochloric acid to give zinc chloride and hydrogen, and copper, which sits below hydrogen, doing nothing with the same acid

examples.title: Why the Bronze Age came first
examples.body:
The order in which people got hold of metals is the reactivity series read backwards, and for a reason rather than by luck.

Gold and copper turn up as metal or come out of their ores in an ordinary fire with charcoal. Iron needs a furnace hot enough and a good deal more carbon. Aluminium is the commonest metal in the Earth's crust and could not be had at all until there was electricity to tear it away from its oxygen. Every step needed a better way of taking the oxygen away.

steps.title: Metals and oxygen
steps.body:
**Metals react with oxygen to produce metal oxides.** These are **oxidation** reactions, because the metals **gain oxygen**.

$$\mathrm{2Mg + O_2 \rightarrow 2MgO}$$

$$\mathrm{4Na + O_2 \rightarrow 2Na_2O}$$

**At this spec point, oxidation and reduction are defined by oxygen:**

- **Oxidation** is **gain of oxygen**
- **Reduction** is **loss of oxygen**

A useful pair to keep straight, because in a single reaction one substance is usually oxidised while another is reduced. When **copper oxide** is heated with **carbon**:

$$\mathrm{2CuO + C \rightarrow 2Cu + CO_2}$$

the **copper oxide loses oxygen**, so it is **reduced**; the **carbon gains oxygen**, so it is **oxidised**.

**How vigorously a metal burns follows the reactivity series.** Magnesium burns with a brilliant white flame; iron burns only as fine filings or wool; copper does not burn, though it does slowly tarnish. That is the same order you meet everywhere else in this topic.

**There is a second, more general definition in terms of electrons**, which is **Higher tier** and comes in the next topic. Until then, *oxidation* means *gained oxygen*.

steps.title: The reactivity series
steps.body:
**When metals react with other substances the metal atoms form positive ions. The reactivity of a metal is related to its tendency to form positive ions.**

That sentence is the explanation for the whole series. A metal that **loses its outer electrons readily** forms a positive ion readily, and is therefore **more reactive**.

**The specification's list**, most reactive first:

**potassium · sodium · lithium · calcium · magnesium · zinc · iron · copper**

**Two non-metals are included**, because they are the useful reference points:

- **Carbon**, between **magnesium** and **zinc**
- **Hydrogen**, between **iron** and **copper**

**Why those two matter.** A metal **below carbon** can be extracted from its oxide by **reduction with carbon** — which is zinc, iron, copper. A metal **above hydrogen** will **displace hydrogen from a dilute acid** — which is potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron. **Copper is below hydrogen**, so copper and dilute acid do not react at all.

So the series is not a list to recite. It is a tool that answers *will this react?* before you try it.

**A limit worth knowing:** the reactions of metals with water and acids here are **at room temperature** and do **not** include reactions with **steam**.

steps.title: Displacement
steps.body:
**A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from a compound.**

The more reactive metal takes the place of the less reactive one, because it forms its positive ion more readily.

$$\mathrm{Mg + CuSO_4 \rightarrow MgSO_4 + Cu}$$

**What you see** is the blue copper sulfate solution **fading** as the magnesium dissolves, and **pink-brown copper** appearing on the metal and settling out.

$$\mathrm{Zn + CuSO_4 \rightarrow ZnSO_4 + Cu}$$

Zinc is also above copper, so this happens too — more slowly, because zinc is less reactive than magnesium.

**The reverse does not happen.** Put copper into magnesium sulfate solution and **nothing occurs**, because copper is **below** magnesium and cannot displace it. That is the single most useful thing about displacement: it runs **downwards** through the series only.

**Deducing an order from results.** The spec asks you to **deduce an order of reactivity of metals based on experimental results**. Given a grid of which metals displace which, the rule is mechanical: if **A displaces B**, then **A is above B**. Work through every pair and the order assembles itself — no prior knowledge of the series needed, which is what makes these questions answerable even with unfamiliar metals.

steps.title: Extracting metals
steps.body:
**Unreactive metals such as gold are found in the Earth as the metal itself.** Gold is so unreactive that it has not combined with anything, so it is found **native** — as nuggets of gold.

**Most metals are found as compounds** that require **chemical reactions to extract the metal**, usually as **oxides**.

**Metals less reactive than carbon can be extracted from their oxides by reduction with carbon.** The carbon takes the oxygen away:

$$\mathrm{2CuO + C \rightarrow 2Cu + CO_2}$$

**Reduction involves the loss of oxygen**, and here it is the **copper oxide** that is reduced.

**So position in the series decides the method:**

- **Below carbon** (zinc, iron, copper) — extract by **reduction with carbon**, which is cheap
- **Above carbon** (potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium) — carbon cannot take the oxygen from them, so **electrolysis** is used instead, which is expensive because it needs a great deal of electricity

**That is why aluminium was a precious metal in the nineteenth century and is now used for drink cans.** Nothing changed about aluminium; what changed was that electrolysis became practical.

**The spec limits this**: knowledge is limited to **reduction of oxides using carbon**, and you do **not** need the details of industrial extraction processes. What you do need is to **interpret or evaluate** an extraction process you are given, and to **identify what is oxidised and what is reduced** in terms of gain or loss of oxygen.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. What is oxidation, in terms of oxygen?
2. Write the reactivity series from potassium to copper.
3. Name a metal that does not react with dilute acid.

**Part B.**

4. Explain what happens when magnesium is added to copper sulfate solution, including what you would see.

**Part C.**

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Reactivity is a tendency to form positive ions, and saying so changes the answer.** A metal reacts by **losing electrons** to become a **positive ion**; the more readily it does that, the more reactive it is. An answer that says *potassium is more reactive than copper* has stated the series; an answer that says *potassium loses its outer electron more readily, so it forms its positive ion more easily* has explained it.

**Carbon and hydrogen are the two lines that make the series a tool.** Below **carbon**: extract with **carbon**. Above **carbon**: **electrolysis**. Above **hydrogen**: reacts with **dilute acid**. Below **hydrogen**: does not. Learn those two positions and a great many questions answer themselves — including questions about metals you have never met, provided you are told where they sit.

**Displacement runs one way.** More reactive displaces less reactive, never the reverse. So a prediction can be checked before it is written: if the reaction you have proposed runs **up** the series, it does not happen. This is also why an experiment showing *no reaction* is **evidence**, not a failure — it tells you the added metal is **below** the one in the compound.

**Deducing an order needs no prior knowledge.** *If A displaces B, A is above B.* Apply that to every pair in a results grid and the order falls out. The metals can be labelled X, Y and Z and the question is still completely answerable, which is exactly why examiners set it that way.

**Two definitions of oxidation, and the question tells you which.** At this point it is **gain of oxygen**; at Higher tier it is **loss of electrons**. Both are correct, and they agree — a metal gaining oxygen is also losing electrons — but an answer should use the one the question is written in.

**The economics follow the chemistry.** Extraction by **carbon reduction** is cheap; **electrolysis** needs a great deal of **electricity** and so is expensive. That is why reactive metals were historically rare and costly, and it is the link a question about cost or about recycling is reaching for.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Metals react with oxygen to produce metal oxides**, and these are **oxidation** reactions.
- At this spec point, **oxidation is gain of oxygen** and **reduction is loss of oxygen**.
- **When metals react, their atoms form positive ions.**
- **Reactivity is the tendency to form positive ions** — how readily the metal loses electrons.
- The series, most reactive first: **potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron, copper**.
- **Carbon** sits between **magnesium and zinc**; **hydrogen** between **iron and copper**.
- Metals **above hydrogen** react with **dilute acid**: potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron.
- **Copper is below hydrogen**, so it does **not** react with dilute acid.
- Reactions with water and acid are at **room temperature** and do **not** include **steam**.
- **A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a compound.**
- Magnesium displaces copper: $\mathrm{Mg + CuSO_4 \rightarrow MgSO_4 + Cu}$ — the blue fades and pink-brown copper appears.
- Displacement runs **downwards** only; the reverse reaction does not happen.
- To **deduce an order**: if **A displaces B**, then **A is above B**.
- **Unreactive metals such as gold** are found **as the metal itself**.
- Metals **below carbon** are extracted by **reduction with carbon**: zinc, iron, copper.
- Metals **above carbon** need **electrolysis**, which is expensive because of the electricity.

questions.prompt: Explain what the reactivity series is, how it is related to the ions metals form, and how it can be used to predict whether a displacement reaction will happen.
questions.solution:
When a metal reacts with another substance, its **atoms form positive ions** — the metal **loses electrons**. The **reactivity of a metal is its tendency to form those positive ions**: a metal that loses its outer electrons readily is **more reactive**, and one that holds them tightly is less so. That single idea is what the whole series is built on.

Arranged most reactive first, the metals in the specification are **potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron, copper**. Two **non-metals** are included as reference points: **carbon**, which sits between magnesium and zinc, and **hydrogen**, between iron and copper. They are there because each marks a line that decides something useful — metals **below carbon** can be extracted from their oxides by **reduction with carbon**, and metals **above hydrogen** will **displace hydrogen from a dilute acid**.

The series predicts **displacement** directly: **a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a compound**. Magnesium is above copper, so adding magnesium to copper sulfate solution gives

$$\mathrm{Mg + CuSO_4 \rightarrow MgSO_4 + Cu}$$

and the blue colour **fades** while **pink-brown copper** appears. The magnesium forms its positive ion more readily than copper does, so it takes copper's place in the compound.

What makes the series a genuine predictive tool is that displacement runs **one way only**. Copper added to magnesium sulfate solution produces **nothing at all**, because copper is **below** magnesium and cannot displace it. This means that a result of **no reaction** is not a failed experiment — it is **evidence**. It tells you the added metal lies **below** the metal in the compound.

That is also how an order can be **deduced from results alone**. The rule is simply *if A displaces B, then A is above B*. Applied to every pair in a grid of results, it assembles the order without any prior knowledge of which metals are involved — which is why such questions can be set using metals labelled only X, Y and Z.

questions.prompt: Explain why different metals are extracted in different ways, using gold, iron and aluminium as examples, and explain what is oxidised and what is reduced when a metal oxide is heated with carbon.
questions.solution:
The method used to extract a metal is decided by **where it sits in the reactivity series**, because that is what determines how strongly it holds on to its oxygen.

**Gold** is at the very bottom, and is so **unreactive** that it has essentially **no tendency to form positive ions**. It has therefore never combined with anything, and is found in the Earth **as the metal itself** — as native nuggets. No extraction reaction is needed at all.

**Iron** is **below carbon** in the series, so it can be extracted from its oxide by **reduction with carbon**. The carbon takes the oxygen away from the metal oxide:

$$\mathrm{2CuO + C \rightarrow 2Cu + CO_2}$$

is the same process for copper, and iron is extracted in the same way in a blast furnace. This route is **cheap**, because carbon in the form of coke is inexpensive and the reaction simply needs heat.

**Aluminium** is **above carbon**. Carbon can only remove the oxygen from a metal **less reactive than itself**, so it cannot reduce aluminium oxide — aluminium holds its oxygen too strongly. Aluminium is therefore extracted by **electrolysis**, which requires a very large amount of **electricity** and is consequently **much more expensive**. This is why aluminium was treated as a precious metal in the nineteenth century and is now used for drink cans: nothing about the chemistry changed, only the practicality of electrolysis.

When a metal oxide is heated with carbon, **both** an oxidation and a reduction happen at once. The **metal oxide loses oxygen**, so it is **reduced**. The **carbon gains oxygen** to become carbon dioxide, so it is **oxidised**. At this point in the course these are the definitions to use — **reduction is loss of oxygen, oxidation is gain of oxygen** — although at Higher tier the same reactions can be described more generally in terms of the **loss and gain of electrons**, and the two descriptions agree.

questions.modelAnswer:
The method used to extract a metal is decided by **where it sits in the reactivity series**, because that is what determines how strongly it holds on to its oxygen.

**Gold** is at the very bottom, and is so **unreactive** that it has essentially **no tendency to form positive ions**. It has therefore never combined with anything, and is found in the Earth **as the metal itself** — as native nuggets. No extraction reaction is needed at all.

**Iron** is **below carbon** in the series, so it can be extracted from its oxide by **reduction with carbon**. The carbon takes the oxygen away from the metal oxide:

$$\mathrm{2CuO + C \rightarrow 2Cu + CO_2}$$

is the same process for copper, and iron is extracted in the same way in a blast furnace. This route is **cheap**, because carbon in the form of coke is inexpensive and the reaction simply needs heat.

**Aluminium** is **above carbon**. Carbon can only remove the oxygen from a metal **less reactive than itself**, so it cannot reduce aluminium oxide — aluminium holds its oxygen too strongly. Aluminium is therefore extracted by **electrolysis**, which requires a very large amount of **electricity** and is consequently **much more expensive**. This is why aluminium was treated as a precious metal in the nineteenth century and is now used for drink cans: nothing about the chemistry changed, only the practicality of electrolysis.

When a metal oxide is heated with carbon, **both** an oxidation and a reduction happen at once. The **metal oxide loses oxygen**, so it is **reduced**. The **carbon gains oxygen** to become carbon dioxide, so it is **oxidised**. At this point in the course these are the definitions to use — **reduction is loss of oxygen, oxidation is gain of oxygen** — although at Higher tier the same reactions can be described more generally in terms of the **loss and gain of electrons**, and the two descriptions agree.

examTechnique.body:
The series is only worth learning if you also learn the **two lines in it**. **Carbon** decides the extraction method; **hydrogen** decides whether dilute acid reacts. Most questions in this topic are one of those two lines applied, or a displacement prediction, which is the same rule again.

When a question gives you **results** rather than names, use the rule *if A displaces B, A is above B* — it works with unfamiliar metals and needs nothing memorised.
examinerErrors: Describing reactivity as *how fast it reacts* rather than as the **tendency to form positive ions**.
Saying copper does not react with acid because it is *unreactive*, rather than because it is **below hydrogen**.
Predicting a displacement that runs **up** the series.
Treating a **no reaction** result as a failed experiment rather than as **evidence**.
Mixing the **oxygen** and **electron** definitions of oxidation in the same answer.
Saying aluminium is expensive because its **ore is rare**, when the reason is **electrolysis**.
Forgetting that **carbon and hydrogen** are in the series, and so losing both useful lines.
Including reactions with **steam**, which this spec point excludes.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer explains the series rather than reciting it: reactivity is the **tendency to form positive ions**, so the order is an order of how readily electrons are lost. It uses **carbon** and **hydrogen** as the two decision lines and can place an unfamiliar metal from two pieces of evidence. It treats **no reaction** as data — proof that a metal sits below another — and deduces a full order from a results grid using nothing but *A displaces B means A is above B*. And it connects the chemistry to the cost: position decides **method**, and method decides **price**, which is why aluminium was once precious.
